title: Adaptive Rational Activations to Boost Deep Reinforcement Learning
authors: Quentin Delfosse, Patrick Schramowski, Martin Mundt, Alejandro Molina, Kristian Kersting
text:
Neural Networks’ efficiency in approximating any function has made them the default choice in many machine learning tasks. This is no different in deep reinforcement learning (RL), where the DQN algorithm’s introduction [1] has sparked the development of various neural solutions. In concurrence with former neuroscientific explanations of brainpower residing in combinations stemming from trillions of connections [2], present advances have emphasised the role of the neural architecture [3,4]. As such, RL improvements have first been mainly obtained through enhancing algorithms [5,6,7] and only recently by searching for performing architectural patterns, via automatic deep policy search [8,9], or via decoupling object detection [10,11] and policy search [12,13].

However, research has also progressively shown that individual neurons shoulder more complexity than initially expected, with the latest results demonstrating that dendritic compartments can compute complex functions (e.g. XOR) [14], previously categorised as unsolvable by single-neuron systems. This finding seems to have renewed interest in activation functions [15,16]. In fact, many functions have been adopted across different domains [17,18,19]. To reduce the bias introduced by a fixed activation function and achieve higher expressive power, one can further learn which activation function is performant for a particular task [20,3], learn to combine arbitrary families of activation functions [21], or find coefficients for polynomial activations as weights to be optimised [22].

Whereas these prior approaches have all contributed to their respective investigated scenarios, there exists a finer approach that elegantly encapsulates the challenges brought on by reinforcement learning problems. Specifically, at each layer, we can learn rational activation functions (ratio of polynomials) [23]. Not only can rationals converge to any continuous function, but they have further been proven to be better approximants than polynomials in terms of convergence [24]. Even more crucially, their ability to adapt while learning equips a model with high neural plasticity (“capability to adjust to the environment and its transformations” [2]). We argue that adapting to environmental changes is essential, making rational activation functions particularly suitable for dynamic RL environments. To provide a visual intuition, we showcase an exemplary evolution of two rational activation functions together with their respective changing input distributions in the dynamic “Time Pilot” environment in Fig. 1.

In this work, we show that plasticity is of major importance for RL agents, as a central element to satisfy the requirements originating from diverse and dynamic environments and propose the use of rational activation functions to augment deep RL agents plasticity. Apart from demonstrating the suitability of adaptive activation functions for Deep RL, we also evaluate how many additional layer weights can be replaced by rational activations. Our specific contributions are:

We motivate why neural plasticity is a key aspect for Deep RL agents and that rational activations are adequate as adaptable activation functions. For this purpose, we not only highlight that rational activation functions adapt their parameters over time, but further prove that they can dynamically embed residual connections, which we refer to as residual plasticity.

As additional representational capacity can hinder generalisation, especially in RL [25,26,27], we propose a joint-rational variant, that uses weight-sharing in rational activations across different layers.

We empirically demonstrate that rational activations bring significant improvements to DQN and Rainbow algorithms on Atari games and that our joint variant further increases performance.

Finally, we investigate the overestimation phenomenon of predicting too large return values, which has previously been argued to originate from an unsuitable representational capacity of the learning architecture [28]. As a result of our introduced (rational) neural and residual plasticity, such overestimation can practically be reduced.

We proceed as follows. We start off by arguing in favour of plasticity for deep RL, then show how rational functions are particularly suitable candidates to provide plasticity in neural networks and present our empirical evaluation. Before concluding, we touch upon related work.
